sentences.text: Ana lived with her mother in a small apartment on the second floor of an old yellow-painted building in Alfama, the oldest neighborhood in Lisbon.
The alley in front of their building was so narrow that if Ana stood at the window and reached out, she could almost touch the building across the way.
The apartment had two rooms and a small balcony where her mother grew basil in a plastic pot.
It was Ana's whole world.
She was ten.
She had lived there her whole life.
Her mother worked as a nurse at a hospital across the river.
Her mother's shifts were long and often at strange hours, and sometimes she came home very late, and sometimes she was already asleep when Ana woke up.
Ana knew how to make her own breakfast and her own supper, and she was not afraid of being alone.
But she had not been sleeping well that autumn.
She would fall asleep, and then wake up at one or two in the morning, and lie there for a long time in the dark, and finally get up and get a glass of water from the kitchen.
That was what happened on the Tuesday night in October when this story starts.
That night Ana got up at 2:47 in the morning.
She checked her phone.
Her mother was still at the hospital.
She would not be home until seven.
Ana drank her water and stood at the kitchen window, which faced down at the alley, and looked out for a while.
It was almost completely dark.
There was one dim streetlamp at the far end of the alley.
Everything was quiet.
Alfama was mostly quiet at three in the morning, which was one of the strange things about a city that everyone thought never slept.
But directly below her window, in the ground floor of her own building, there was a warm gold light coming out of the small window of the bakery.
Ana knew the bakery.
It had been there her whole life.
It was called Padaria Mendes.
It sold small round breads and custard tarts and coffee, and it opened at seven in the morning and closed at three in the afternoon.
Ana had walked past it a thousand times.
She had never seen it open at any other hour.
Never once.
But now, at three in the morning, the light was on.
She could see, through the window, the shape of a person moving inside.
Ana thought about it for maybe ten minutes.
She was not supposed to leave the apartment alone at night.
Her mother had told her this many times.
But the bakery was right underneath her — one flight of stairs, five meters of cobblestone, and she would be at the door.
She could see it from her own window.
It was not really going out.
Not exactly.
She put on her cardigan and her slippers.
She went down the stairs very quietly.
The building was completely silent.
She unlocked the front door of the building and stepped out into the cool alley.
She walked the five steps to the bakery window.
She pressed her face against the glass.
Inside, an old man with white hair and a flour-dusted apron was kneading a large round of dough on a wooden work surface.
He did not see her at first.
She stood there for a while.
Then he looked up, and he saw her, and he smiled a small tired smile, and he beckoned her in.
She was surprised at how not-surprised he seemed.
The bakery inside smelled like the best thing Ana had ever smelled.
Warm flour and yeast and something like burnt sugar.
The old man kept working.
He said, in a gentle voice, "Come in, come in.
Close the door.
It gets cold.
Are you the girl from upstairs." Ana nodded.
She said, "I am Ana.
I live on the second floor." "Ana," said the old man.
"I am Senhor Mendes.
I know your mother.
She has bought bread from me for many years.
You have bought bread from me too, when you were smaller.
I remember when you could barely see over this counter."
Ana did remember Senhor Mendes now.
He was the man who sold her the pão when she came in after school.
But she had never really looked at him.
He had just been the bakery man.
Now she looked at him.
He was older than she had realized.
His hands were very big and very red at the knuckles, and there was flour up to his elbows.
His eyes were kind but they were also tired.
Very tired.
"Why are you awake," said Senhor Mendes.
Ana said, "I do not sleep very well.
I saw your light.
I did not know the bakery was open at night." Senhor Mendes smiled.
"It is not open," he said.
"Not to customers.
But every day at midnight, I come in and I start.
I have been doing this for fifty-one years.
The bread we sell in the morning starts at midnight.
All night I work.
All night.
Then at six in the morning the first customers come and I open the door, and by three in the afternoon I am done, and I go home and sleep.
Then at midnight I come back.
That has been my life."
"That is a strange life," Ana said.
She said it without thinking.
She was worried immediately that she had been rude.
But Senhor Mendes laughed.
"Yes," he said.
"It is a strange life.
Very strange.
I do not know many people who work at night.
But someone has to make the bread.
It cannot happen while everyone else is awake.
There is not time.
So — I do it.
You get used to being awake at night.
There is a certain calm to it.
You should feel this calm, since you are also awake at three in the morning.
This is when we know things that people asleep do not know."
